job.style: a short story where children solve a real problem

passage: Rohan and Meera were helping their teacher organize the school stationery cupboard. They found a box of pens and pencils. Meera noted that each pen costs 5 rupees more than a pencil. She wrote the relationship as p = q + 5, where p is the cost of a pen and q is the cost of a pencil. Rohan argued that if they had two equations, they could find the exact costs. They looked at a graph showing two lines representing different sets of prices. One line showed the cost of pens and pencils, while the other represented a bulk discount offer. The lines intersected at a single point, (15, 10), which meant a pen costs 15 rupees and a pencil costs 10 rupees. Rohan noticed that the lines extended infinitely in both directions, covering all possible values, including negative ones if they were dealing with abstract coordinates. He realized that a single linear equation has infinitely many solutions, but a pair of equations with different slopes has only one unique solution where they meet. He carefully checked that the point (15, 10) satisfied both equations, confirming it was the correct solution for the pair. They finished their work, happy to see that the intersection point provided the precise cost for both items.

items.evidence: He realized that a single linear equation has infinitely many solutions, but a pair of equations with different slopes has only one unique solution where they meet.
items.q: If Meera uses only p = q + 5, how many price pairs fit it?
options: Infinitely many pairs fit this equation
Exactly one pair fits this equation
Only positive whole-number pairs fit it
No pair fits until a second equation
items.explain: A single linear equation has infinitely many solutions; only a pair of equations gives one unique solution.

wrong.why: thinks one linear equation has only one solution
thinks only whole or positive pairs count
mixes up solutions of one equation with a pair's solution

items.evidence: He carefully checked that the point (15, 10) satisfied both equations, confirming it was the correct solution for the pair.
items.q: Rohan checked the point (15, 10) carefully. What must a solution of a pair do?
options: Satisfy each of the two equations
Satisfy at least one of the equations
Give the correct value of x only
Lie close to one of the lines
items.explain: Rohan confirmed (15, 10) was the pair's solution only after it satisfied both equations.

wrong.why: thinks fitting one equation is enough
thinks a solution is just the x-value
thinks a point near a line counts

items.evidence: The lines intersected at a single point, (15, 10), which meant a pen costs 15 rupees and a pencil costs 10 rupees.
items.q: The two lines meet at (15, 10). What prices does this point give?
options: Pen 15 rupees, pencil 10 rupees
Pen 10 rupees, pencil 15 rupees
Pen 15 rupees, pencil price still unknown
Pen 20 rupees, pencil 15 rupees
items.explain: The first number is the pen's cost and the second is the pencil's: 15 and 10 rupees.

wrong.why: thinks the order in the pair does not matter
thinks the solution is only the first number
wrongly adds 5 again to the point's values

items.evidence: Rohan noticed that the lines extended infinitely in both directions, covering all possible values, including negative ones if they were dealing with abstract coordinates.
items.q: Rohan plots only three points of an equation. What does its full graph show?
options: A line going on endlessly both ways
Only the three dots that were plotted
A line ending at the last plotted point
A line covering only the positive values
items.explain: The graph of a linear equation is a line extending infinitely in both directions, even through negative values.

wrong.why: thinks the graph is just the plotted points
thinks the line stops where plotting stops
thinks only positive values are solutions

items.evidence: Rohan argued that if they had two equations, they could find the exact costs.
items.q: Why did Rohan want a second equation besides p = q + 5?
options: Because one equation cannot fix exact prices
Because one equation has no solutions at all
Because one equation gives only the pen's price
Because two lines always meet at one point
items.explain: One equation has many possible price pairs; two equations together give the exact costs.

wrong.why: thinks a single equation has no solution
thinks a solution is one number, not a pair
thinks any two lines always meet at a point
